channel.title: Computer Chronicle
channel.description: A weekly early-1980s computer newspaper rebuilt from the historical record — games, software, hardware, prices, charts, and culture, one week at a time.

item.title: Week of August 20-26, 1984 — IBM's PC/AT Pushes Personal Computing Into a New Generation
item.description: The 80286-powered 5170 brings a 16-bit expansion path, a 1.2MB floppy, larger storage, and prices beginning at $3,995. IBM's Personal Computer AT dominates the conversation as the week opens. Announced August 14, the machine type 5170 is built around Intel's 80286, with a 16-bit data path and 24-bit addressing. IBM says it performs more than twice as fast as current members of the PC family, a claim that marks a clean break from the original 8088 generation. Also this week: Software Becomes the Home-Computer Show's Main Event · Low-Cost Adapters Put Atari and Apple Owners on the Line · Infocom Sends Adventurers Diving for Treasure in Cutthroats.

item.title: Week of August 13-19, 1984 — IBM's PC/AT Opens a Second Generation of Personal Computing
item.description: IBM unveils the 80286-powered 5170 with a 16-bit expansion path, high-capacity floppy, larger hard disks, and prices starting at $3,995. IBM used August 14 to introduce two models of the Personal Computer AT, a machine it says runs more than twice as fast as the current PC family. Both are built around Intel's 80286, with a 24-bit address path and a 16-bit data path that moves the IBM line decisively beyond the original 8088 generation. Also this week: DOS 3.0 and PC Network Prepare IBM Machines to Share · Home-Computer Adventures Hook a Growing Adult Audience.

item.title: Week of August 6-12, 1984 — Behind Closed Doors, Amiga's Lorraine Points to a New Generation
item.description: A rough but dazzling 68000 prototype promises color, sound, animation, speech, and communications in one home machine. Visitors invited behind closed doors at the Summer Consumer Electronics Show saw something very different from another beige box. Amiga's Lorraine prototype, now detailed in COMPUTE!'s August issue, paired a Motorola 68000 processor with custom graphics and sound hardware intended to make animation, music, and multitasking central parts of personal computing. Also this week: Symphony and Framework Fight to Define Integrated Software · Compaq Deskpro Turns Compatibility into a Speed Contest · Questprobe Sends the Hulk into the Adventure Machine · IBM's Price Cuts Put PC-Compatible Makers in a Squeeze.

item.title: Week of July 30-August 5, 1984 — Free Software Travels the Phone Lines
item.description: Thousands of public-domain programs are moving through online services and local bulletin boards, challenging the idea that every useful disk must arrive in a shrink-wrapped box. A Macintosh communications program has become the calling card for a much wider movement. MIT-trained consultant Dennis Brothers wrote MacTEP after probing the new machine closely enough to make it talk over telephone lines, then gave the program away. CompuServe placed it before a reported 135,000 subscribers, and calls soon reached Brothers from Britain and the Dominican Republic. Also this week: Tramiel Takes Atari and the Ax Falls · A Fantasy Computer Game Becomes a Novel · BYTE Surveys the Small-System Frontier.

item.title: Week of July 23-29, 1984 — Activision Forces 'Cuthbert in the Jungle' Off the Market
item.description: A High Court undertaking pulls Microdeal's Commodore 64 game from sale and makes the young software trade confront the difference between inspiration and imitation. LONDON — Activision has forced Microdeal to withdraw Cuthbert in the Jungle after bringing High Court proceedings that alleged the Commodore 64 title copied Pitfall!, Popular Computing Weekly reported on July 26. Microdeal gave the court an undertaking that it would no longer produce the game in any form and notified suppliers that the title could no longer be sold. Also this week: Tramiel's Atari Shake-Up Reaches Britain · Apple Plans to Double Macintosh Production · A Computer Fantasy Game Becomes an Alan Dean Foster Novel.

item.title: Week of July 16-22, 1984 — FBI Seizes Home Computers in Huntsville Hacker Probe
item.description: Four Alabama homes yield computers and related equipment as federal investigators examine unauthorized entry into two systems. HUNTSVILLE, Ala. — Federal agents seized computers and related equipment Monday at four homes in the Huntsville area, an unusually vivid sign that the expanding world of home terminals and dial-up experimentation has begun to draw the close attention of law enforcement. Also this week: Tramiel Takes Atari Into a New, Hard-Cost Era · Imagine Software's Million-Pound Dream Bursts · Apple IIc Brings 128K and Plug-In Simplicity Home · £1.99 Games Ignite a British Software Price War.

item.title: Week of July 9-15, 1984 — Atari-Commodore Rivalry Turns into a Fight over Trade Secrets
item.description: Days after Jack Tramiel takes control of Atari’s consumer operation, his old rivalry with Commodore shifts from price cuts and product launches to engineers, designs and the courts. The struggle for the home-computer market acquired a legal edge this week. On July 14, The New York Times reported a dispute over Commodore trade secrets, arriving only days after Warner Communications transferred Atari’s home-computer and video-game businesses to a company led by former Commodore chief Jack Tramiel. Also this week: BYTE Puts Computers and Video in the Spotlight · Sinclair Warns QL Buyers of Delivery Delays · PC Magazine Surveys a Fast-Growing IBM Ecosystem.

item.title: Week of July 2-8, 1984 — Jack Tramiel Takes Atari as Warner Retreats
item.description: The Commodore founder acquires Atari's home-computer and console operations, setting up a fierce new round in the personal-computer price war. Warner Communications sold Atari's loss-plagued home-computer and home-video-game operations on Monday, July 2, to a new company headed by Jack Tramiel. Warner kept the coin-operated arcade operation, while the consumer business became the foundation of a new Atari Corporation. Also this week: Apple IIc Packs a Full Apple II into 7.5 Pounds · The Hulk Leads Atari's Living Software Shelf · Byte Watches Computers and Video Converge.

item.title: Week of June 25-July 1, 1984 — AT&T Enters the Personal-Computer Market with the PC 6300
item.description: The post-divestiture telephone giant puts an 8 MHz 8086 machine into the crowded IBM-compatible business market. AT&T Information Systems entered the personal-computer market in New York on Tuesday, June 26, placing one of America's largest technology names directly in the path of IBM and the multiplying compatible makers. Its PC 6300 is an AT&T-branded version of Olivetti's M24, built to run software written for the IBM PC. Also this week: Printer Buyers Face a Maze from Dot Matrix to Laser · VisiCorp Tries to Regain Its Business-Software Footing · Timex/Sinclair Owners Build a Lifeline on CompuServe.

item.title: Week of June 18-24, 1984 — MIT's Project Athena Opens a New Window
item.description: Robert Scheifler announces the X Window System, separating graphical programs from the screens that display them. Robert Scheifler at MIT's Project Athena announced the X Window System on June 19, giving the laboratory's networked workstations a new way to draw and manage graphical displays. The first implementation was written for a VAX VS100, but its central idea reaches beyond a single machine. Also this week: VisiCorp Tries to Re-enter the Business-Software Race · Apple IIc Packs the Apple II into 7.5 Pounds · Stolen Password Exposes the Fragility of Online Credit Files.

item.title: Week of June 11-17, 1984 — Police Seize a Bulletin Board: Is the Sysop Liable for What Users Post?
item.description: Los Angeles authorities confiscate MOG-UR’s HBBS equipment after telephone access codes appear among user messages. Los Angeles police have seized the computer equipment behind MOG-UR’s HBBS, thrusting a three-year-old hobbyist bulletin board into an unfamiliar legal contest over responsibility for messages left by users. Pacific Telephone security investigators alerted police after finding a telephone credit-card code and two Sprint access numbers among posts on the system. Also this week: Fido Wants to Travel: Hobbyist Boards Begin to Form a Network · Novelists Move from Type to Bytes at Summer CES · Morrow's Pivot Puts a PC-Compatible Computer on a Shoulder Strap · Apple IIc Interest Runs Ahead of Complete Systems.

item.title: Week of June 4-10, 1984 — IBM Cuts Prices Across the PC Line
item.description: Lower tags on personal computers, drives, displays and adapters turn up the pressure in an increasingly crowded compatible market. IBM moved to sharpen its position in personal computing this week with price reductions across portions of the PC line. The changes reached beyond a single box: the company’s June hardware list covered the PC, XT, Portable PC, disk drives, displays and adapters, giving dealers and buyers a fresh schedule for assembling complete systems. Also this week: Postal Service Votes to Abandon E-COM · Computer Games Start Learning New Tricks · Copy Protection Draws Fire from Paying Customers.

item.title: Week of May 28-June 3, 1984 — Comdex/Spring Shows the Micro Market Still Surging
item.description: Atlanta fills with 851 suppliers, IBM-compatible machines and a new contest to put every office task inside one package. Comdex/Spring opened on a scale that made the personal-computer boom impossible to miss. Computerworld counted 851 suppliers, 158 of them first-time exhibitors, and expected well over 45,000 visitors. The aisles offered a working map of an industry still multiplying around the IBM PC standard. Also this week: Framework Bets $695 That Ideas Belong in an Outline · Delayed Windows Leaves PC Software on Islands · TeleVideo Puts PCs Around an $8,995 Multiuser Hub.

item.title: Week of May 21-27, 1984 — Atari Bets on Compatibility with $140 7800 ProSystem
item.description: A sharper arcade-style machine promises to preserve the vast Atari 2600 cartridge shelf. Atari unveiled the 7800 ProSystem on May 21, pitching a $140 console as the company’s answer to a home videogame business shaken by falling sales and crowded store shelves. The new machine promised more elaborate arcade-style action while meeting owners on familiar ground: it could also play Atari 2600 cartridges. Also this week: Ashton-Tate Unwraps dBASE III for IBM PCs · NEC Breaks the $2,000 Barrier for a Complete 16-bit Business Micro · Telemail Intrusions Put Online Security on the Front Page.

item.title: Week of May 14-20, 1984 — Telenet Locks the Dial-Up Door
item.description: A new device promises to bar unauthorized callers from computer systems reached over telephone lines. WASHINGTON — GTE Telenet introduced a device Tuesday, May 15, designed to lock unauthorized users out of computer systems reached through telephone lines. The announcement turns the fast-growing worry over modem intrusion into a commercial hardware market. Also this week: Atari Pledges a Sober XL Comeback · Lucasfilm Turns Its Cameras Toward Games · Sub-$100 Modems Call the Home Office.

item.title: Week of May 7-13, 1984 — Lucasfilm Brings the Force to Home Videogames
item.description: The film studio unveils Ballblazer and Rescue on Fractalus!, two Atari projects built around fresh technology and a cinematic sense of play. SAN RAFAEL, Calif. — Lucasfilm publicly entered the home videogame market May 8, unveiling the first two projects from a Games Group nurtured through its collaboration with Atari. The announcement puts one of cinema's most famous technical workshops behind software intended for Atari 8-bit computers and the 5200 console. Also this week: Pens and Tablets Challenge the Keyboard · Home Word Processing Drops Below $100 · Atari Searches for a New Mission.

item.title: Week of April 30-May 6, 1984 — Hanover's 650,000 Visitors See the Portable Future
item.description: Epson lifts the lid on a lap-size LCD machine as Commodore signals a 16-bit business turn. HANOVER, West Germany — One of Europe's largest computer fairs drew roughly 650,000 visitors this week, turning the exhibition floor into a vivid measure of how quickly electronic computing is moving from specialist rooms toward desks, briefcases and homes. Also this week: Chuck Peddle Rides Back to Victor with the PlusPC · One Box, Two Computer Worlds · Can a Computer Teach Music? · Early Macintosh Verdict: Brilliant, but Boxed In.

item.title: Week of April 23-29, 1984 — Apple Puts the II in a Carrying Case
item.description: The $1,295 Apple IIc brings 128K, a built-in disk drive and nearly a decade of Apple II software into a compact 7.5-pound package. SAN FRANCISCO — Apple Computer unveiled the Apple IIc on April 24 at its “Apple II Forever” dealer convention, putting the durable Apple II design into an ivory case small enough to carry by its handle. Even a 6.2-magnitude earthquake shaking Moscone Center could not upstage the week’s landmark personal-computer announcement. Also this week: Apple II Forever, Apple III No More · IBM’s PCjr Stumbles Out of the Gate · Software Becomes the Machine’s Magic · April’s Game Shelf Spans Machines.

item.title: Week of April 16-22, 1984 — Software Steps Into the Spotlight
item.description: TIME puts the programs inside the machine on its April 16 cover as applications, compatibility and ease of use begin deciding the personal-computer contest. The personal-computer business has spent years selling the wonder of the machine itself. This week, the spotlight swings decisively to the programs that make those machines useful. TIME’s April 16 cover story, “The Wizard Inside the Machine,” calls software the magic carpet to the future and captures an industry learning that specifications alone do not close the sale. Also this week: Macintosh Meets the User-Group Crowd · Atari Sends Arcade Names to Rival Machines · PCjr and Macintosh Court the Newcomer.

item.title: Week of April 9-15, 1984 — HomeWord Brings Icons to Three Computer Camps
item.description: Sierra On-Line gives Apple, Commodore 64 and Atari owners the same $49.95 picture-guided word processor. A filing cabinet, a printed page, a printer, a disorderly page with an arrow, a question mark and a floppy disk now stand between the home writer and the command line. Sierra On-Line has introduced HomeWord for the Apple, Commodore 64 and Atari families, using six pictured icons to guide the program's principal jobs. Also this week: Atari's Games Defect to the Competition · War Games Grow Up on the Commodore 64 · The $100 Home Computer Is No Longer a Fantasy · Color Graphics Become a $39.95 C64 Tool.
